articles.title: Ex-White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172,000 for Trump speech bets
articles.summary: The staffer was found to have used his prior knowledge of the president's speeches to place lucrative bets.
articles.body:
A former White House teleprompter operator has been ordered to pay more than $172,000 (£127,000) for using inside information to bet on US President Donald Trump's speeches.

Gabriel Perez was found to have made trades on what the president would say during addresses between December 2025 and February 2026 on Kalshi - a prediction markets platform where users can bet on real-world events.

Its regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), said Perez would have to surrender profits of $107,539.02 (£79,452) and pay a civil penalty of $65,000 (£48,000).

The White House has not yet commented. In July, then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Perez was on unpaid leave and would not return to his post.

Announcing the settlement on Friday, the CFTC said Perez had "misappropriated" his prior knowledge of Trump's speeches to place bets "in breach of his duty of trust and confidence".

It said his civil penalty had been reduced due to his "exemplary co-operation" with the investigation.

Perez has also been banned from trading for three years.

Writing on X, Kalshi's lead lawyer Bobby DeNault welcomed the decision: "It doesn't matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences."

The company previously told the BBC its analysts had noticed unusual betting on "mention markets" – contracts where users predict whether a speaker will use common terms, such as specific countries, campaign slogans or words – in March.

It said it had used account data to find that the user was a federal employee operating White House teleprompters, and had reported the activity to the regulator.

"The words of political leaders like Presidents and Fed chairs cause billions of dollars of movement in FX markets, oil futures, [and] the stock market," it said in a statement in July.

The same month, the White House Management Office had sent a letter to aides telling them not to place bets on prediction markets, administration officials told the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

articles.title: Dem candidate erupts in profane defense of Hasan Piker as party figures distance themselves

articles.title: 'We have not slowed down': Minnesota not out of the woods on massive fraud scandal, expert warns
articles.summary: Despite Minnesota's fraud scandal costing taxpayers billions, a policy expert warns more than one new assisted-living license is approved daily.
articles.body: Despite Minnesota’s fraud scandal exploding onto the national scene and costing taxpayers billions, there are growing concerns that the state has still not done what’s necessary to root out the problem. "We have not slowed down, there is no sense in which the fraud has been stopped in Minnesota," Bill Glahn, a policy fellow at the Center of the American Experiment, told Fox News Digital. Glahn has been warning on social media that Minnesota’s rapid growth in provisional assisted-living licenses, most for small facilities, may be outpacing state oversight. In a recent article, Glahn explained the state’s licensing database showed 364 new facilities with provisional licenses popping up over the past year and called for a 90-day moratorium on new licenses while officials investigate. "We have something along the order of 2,500 of these licensed across the state, but about 20% of them, around three, 400 of them have just been started in the last year," Glahn explained. FINAL WALZ FRAUD REPORT RIPS ‘CULTURE OF TOLERANCE’ AS MINNESOTA TAXPAYERS FACE BILLIONS IN ALLEGED LOSSES "I'm not sure if there's a real underlying driver in the demographics or the demand for these facilities, but it's odd that we have these assisted living facilities linked to Medicaid fraud, at the same time, the Minnesota Department of Health is approving more than one a day. More than one new facility gets approved every single day, 365 days a year. And I don't think anybody is really giving any thought to, hey, maybe some of this is not on the up and up." Glahn also pointed to a recent criminal complaint filed by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison’s office against Salman Ahmed Elmi, who was charged Aug. 17 with eight felony theft offenses tied to alleged Medicaid billing fraud, as evidence that fraud is still taking place. The criminal complaint also details alleged ties among the Medicaid-funded businesses, properties previously used to provide commercial sex services and people investigators say were part of a sex-trafficking organization. FAILED PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE WINS DEM PRIMARY FOR MIDWEST GOVERNOR AMID FRAUD SCANDAL FALLOUT "This is two scandals in one," Glahn said. "You have a commercial sex operation, actual brothels, housed in what were later licensed as assisted-living facilities under the Medicaid program." Elmi previously received an award from the state for being an "Outstanding Refugee." "Elmi’s case alone makes clear that this is not old news," Glahn said. "This particular fraud was going on just a couple of months ago." Glahn argued that the latest allegations point to a deeper problem within the state agencies responsible for vetting providers and monitoring taxpayer-funded programs which haven’t been properly addressed. "Personnel is policy," Glahn said. "There isn’t a regulatory mindset under the Walz administration. There isn’t the mindset that we need to trust but verify." While Minnesota officials and lawmakers have taken some fraud-prevention steps since the fraud scandal erupted onto the national scene, Glahn stressed that the reforms do not address what he sees as the central issue: a lack of accountability for those who failed to identify the schemes earlier "Walz has never cleaned house, he’s never fired anybody for not detecting the fraud or not prosecuting the fraud," Glahn said. "It’s the same people doing the same thing, and that culture has never changed." For Glahn, the messaging should start at the top. "They're just operating as business as usual," Glahn said. "We don't have anybody who's currently in office, currently in charge of state government, at least in the executive branch, who's doing anything substantive to address the fraud. It's just amazing how we see these reports every day, and we have Tim Walz traveling the country, traveling elsewhere. He's a lame duck. He doesn't seem to have any interest in closing out this chapter of his legacy with any kind of victory on the fraud front." MILLION-DOLLAR SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD SCHEME IN WALZ'S BACKYARD SPARKS OUTRAGE: 'CRUEL JOKE' In addition to the perception that not enough accountability has been taken for the scandal, Walz's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is running for Senate while Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar is running for governor despite both being in positions of power during the duration of time the fraud scandal festered. "Amy Klobuchar has come out with her multi-point plan of how she's gonna fight fraud once she gets in office, if she gets elected in November," Glahn explained. "I don't know why we couldn't implement this stuff today. She's called for a top-to-bottom audit of state government. She's got another few data points that perhaps were legislative proposals that didn't get passed. Tim Walz could call a special session. We could be in session on Monday, passing an anti-fraud agenda, but there's nothing. So I guess he just fundamentally doesn't have an interest in the subject." Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office, Klobuchar's campaign and the Minnesota Department of Health for comment but did not receive a response. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Minnesota Department of Human Services told Fox News Digital in a statement that it has rolled out a series of anti-fraud reforms since the fall of 2024, including identifying 14 high-risk services and freezing the enrollment of new providers in those programs. The agency also said it discontinued the Housing Stabilization Services program, began auditing autism-service providers through onsite visits, instituted licensure requirements for autism centers and disenrolled inactive providers. DHS said it has also expanded pre-payment reviews for providers in 13 high-risk fee-for-service programs and completed revalidation determinations for high-risk providers by the end of May. Since the beginning of 2025, the department said it has stopped payments to 747 Medicaid providers over what it described as credible allegations of fraud and made 824 referrals to law enforcement.

articles.title: La promesa de Trump con la Humanidad antes del cierre de su segundo mandato
articles.standfirst: Asegura que antes de las elecciones estadounidenses de 2028 el hombre volverá a pisar la Luna
articles.summary: Asegura que antes de las elecciones estadounidenses de 2028 el hombre volverá a pisar la Luna
articles.body: El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, anunció en Houston su intención de que la humanidad vuelva a pisar la Luna antes de que concluya su segundo mandato en 2028. El anuncio tuvo lugar durante un acto de homenaje a la tripulación de la misión Artemis II, que sobrevoló la Luna en abril de 2026. Durante su intervención, Trump aseguró que Estados Unidos trabaja ya en proyectos vinculados a la presencia permanente en el satélite, incluida una futura colonia lunar. También destacó los avances de la NASA en el desarrollo de una nave espacial de propulsión nuclear destinada a una futura misión a Marte. "Vamos a tener una colonia. De hecho la están construyendo ahí arriba, en la Luna... La NASA, ya ha comenzado a trabajar en la primera nave espacial interplanetaria de propulsión nuclear, que se lanzará en 2028 en una misión a Marte", explicaba. Asimismo, el mandatario presentó otro de los proyectos de su Administración en el ámbito espacial: la creación de una Academia Espacial de Estados Unidos. Según explicó, esta institución tendrá como objetivo formar a militares, ingenieros y especialistas para las necesidades de la Fuerza Espacial y del sector aeroespacial. "Necesitamos educar y capacitar a toda una generación de militares, ingenieros y operadores civiles cualificados, emitiremos una orden ejecutiva para iniciar el proceso de creación de una nueva academia nacional: la Academia Espacial de Estados Unidos", indicaba al respecto el mandatario estadounidense. La nueva academia sería la primera institución académica militar de nueva creación desde la fundación de la Academia de la Fuerza Aérea en 1954. Trump confirmó la puesta en marcha del proyecto mediante la firma de una orden ejecutiva durante el mismo evento celebrado en el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA, en Texas. En conjunto, los anuncios refuerzan la apuesta de la Administración estadounidense por el desarrollo de la exploración espacial, con objetivos centrados en la Luna, Marte y la formación de personal especializado para futuras misiones y operaciones espaciales.

articles.title: Democrats on campaign trail divided by Kamala Harris
articles.summary: Democratic candidates in competitive election races are taking different tacks this cycle over how close to affiliate themselves with former Vice President Kamala Harris, who’s lent her support to many of them but whose loss in the 2024 election has made her a more polarizing figure. Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D) told reporters this…
articles.body:
Democratic candidates in competitive election races are taking different tacks this cycle over how close to affiliate themselves with former Vice President Kamala Harris, who’s lent her support to many of them but whose loss in the 2024 election has made her a more polarizing figure.

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek (D) told reporters this week he didn’t want Harris to campaign for him as he pursues a Senate seat this cycle — a sentiment Iowa gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, the state’s auditor, also shared about Harris and former President Biden.

Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s (D-Alaska) Senate campaign also voiced frustration after Harris’s PAC issued a fundraising email for the red-state Democrat earlier this month.

But not all Democrats are keeping Harris at arm’s length.

The former vice president joined a Women for Ossoff call set up by Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-Ga.) reelection campaign. She also made a fundraising appeal on his Facebook page.

And Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said he was “grateful” to have Harris’s support after she endorsed him following his primary.

While the different tactics likely reflect the political realities of red and purple states, they’ve also raised questions about Harris’s political viability as she mulls a second presidential run.

“The VP did very well in some places and didn’t do great in others, and if you’re in a state where she didn’t perform well, it may not help you to have her campaign with you this fall,” said Democratic strategist Jamal Simmons, who served as Harris’s communications director in the vice president’s office.

“Each candidate has a different problem they’re trying to solve,” Simmons added.

Democratic strategist Anthony Coley, who worked for the Biden administration, says that to win in red states, Democratic candidates have to “distinguish themselves from a national Democratic brand that is deeply unpopular.”

“As the party’s most recent presidential nominee, Kamala Harris is closely tied to that brand,” Coley said.

“Harris still has a deep reservoir of goodwill among many Democrats. But this … speaks to the tough political terrain outside blue states and to the work Harris must do to recast herself as a populist, antiestablishment fighter if she wants to run for president again and expand the electoral map,” Coley added.

In a state like Michigan — particularly in the competitive Senate race — some Democrats point out Harris’s presence could be more of a problem for candidates.

“She is a huge liability,” said John Morgan, the Democratic mega-donor, adding that anyone “who has a shot to win” would want to steer clear.

“Look what happened in Alaska,” he said, referring to Harris’s PAC appeal on behalf of Peltola and how Republicans have used it to tie Harris to the candidate.

One Democratic strategist, who asked for anonymity to give a candid assessment, pointed to the electoral map in 2024.

“Look, the reality is, she underperformed in Michigan, particularly in places like Dearborn,” said the strategist, who has been involved in recent presidential elections. “And Elissa Slotkin was on the ballot and won. So that says a lot.”

“I think you’d rather have surrogates who can help,” they added.

The strategist said Harris could be an asset to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in his Senate race in places like the state’s Research Triangle, the area in central North Carolina that covers Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill, and the parts between.

“I could see her being welcome or at least not unwelcome,” they said.

Harris has offered endorsements or issued fundraising emails toward a host of Democrats running in competitive elections this cycle, ranging from Peltola to Arkansas House candidate Chris Jones to Maine Senate candidate Troy Jackson.

In some cases, Democrats have welcomed her efforts — both public and private — to support them.

“Senator Ossoff is grateful for Vice President Harris’ help and support in his re-election campaign,” an Ossoff campaign spokesperson told The Hill.

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan’s (D) Senate campaign noted the former vice president contacted her after her primary win.

“Peggy was proud to campaign for Vice President Harris and appreciated her calling to congratulate her following her primary victory,” a Flanagan campaign spokesperson told The Hill. “Peggy values her relationship with Vice President Harris and remains focused on the leadership Minnesotans are looking for — a fighter who will take on the Trump administration and its reckless abuses of power.”

Jones, who’s running for Arkansas’s 2nd Congressional District, said in a statement he was “honored” to have Harris’s endorsement, adding that “her support means a great deal to this campaign and to the people of AR-02.”

El-Sayed also called Harris’s support “critical.” And while he was a part of the “Uncommitted” movement — where Democratic voters cast “uncommitted” votes instead of voting for then-presidential candidate Biden in Democratic primaries in 2024 as a way to voice frustration over the administration’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war — his statement noted he ultimately backed her in the 2024 election.

Simmons said Harris could easily go to Detroit to help “close the gap” with Black voters in Michigan, a group El-Sayed is eager to court for the general election.

Georgia Democratic strategist Fred Hicks said it makes sense that Ossoff would also welcome the former vice president’s support given that Black voters, particularly Black women, make up a core bloc of the Democratic base in the Peach State.

But some Democrats have notably pushed away the idea of Harris supporting them in their races.

“No thanks,” Sand told Politico in a recent interview when asked whether Biden or Harris should campaign for him. “Let’s move on. We need some new leadership.”

Turek also offered a short “no” and a chuckle when he was asked about what he thought of Sand’s comments, shooting down the idea of Harris campaigning for him.

Peltola, who is battling to topple Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in Alaska, also did not appreciate Harris’s political group, Fight for the People PAC, issuing the fundraising appeal on her behalf.

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” her campaign told The New York Times earlier this month.

Some Senate candidates, meanwhile, haven’t acknowledged Harris’s support. Jackson, Cooper and Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) have said little publicly about the former vice president’s support for them, though several of them backed her 2024 bid.

Democratic strategist Maria Cardona cautioned against reading too much into the reactions toward Harris, saying it was “so early for anyone to take any one little thing and try to read tea leaves into what that means for 2028.”

Cardona suggested the reactions were more about the political dynamics playing out across the country, saying the same situation would play out if a Democrat was in the White House and offering to campaign for their candidates during the midterms.

“What we all want here is for our candidates to win no matter where they are,” she said. “And so I think that no one is going to be taking this personally.”

But Hicks suggested candidates may be wary of encouraging Harris’s support lest it be seen as an implicit endorsement — or obligation to endorse — the former vice president if she runs for the White House in 2028, saying “people do not want to be seen as taking a side in 2028.”

“It’s not as much about the past as it is about the future.”

articles.title: Crackdown on critical tech could open Americans to a new national security threat
articles.summary: Brittany Kaiser warns that data center moratoriums could force American companies to process sensitive data overseas, raising national security concerns.
articles.body: Americans' sensitive information could increasingly be processed overseas if restrictions on artificial intelligence data centers slow construction in the U.S., a data privacy advocate and industry executive warned. The warning comes as states and local governments weigh new restrictions on the rapidly expanding data center industry amid concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and other impacts on surrounding communities. Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, said state moratoriums and restrictions on new data centers could push American companies to seek computing capacity in other countries as demand from AI continues to surge. "One of my top concerns as a top data protection and privacy advocate is that with data center moratoriums being passed in the United States that it will force Americans and American companies to send our data to be processed abroad in other countries," Kaiser told Fox News Digital. "American companies are going to still run their AI," she added. "They're still going to be purchasing data center space in other countries, and it means our sensitive information will be sent abroad and shared with companies and organizations that might not have America's best interests at heart." FROM NETFLIX TO GPS: 10 WAYS THIS HIDDEN TECH INFRASTRUCTURE QUIETLY POWERS MODERN LIFE Data centers are large facilities filled with servers and computing equipment that process, store and transmit information behind many everyday technologies. They support everything from email, social media and internet searches to online banking, streaming services and AI platforms. As demand for AI grows, companies are building increasingly powerful data centers that require vast amounts of electricity, advanced chips and high-speed network connections. Kaiser said the facilities have become critical infrastructure for the digital economy, making decisions about where they are built and who controls the data they handle a matter of growing economic and national security concern. Artificial intelligence, however, requires significantly more computing power, fueling a rapid expansion of data center construction across the country. That growth has sparked pushback in some communities over concerns about electricity costs, water consumption, noise and environmental impacts. Kaiser acknowledged those concerns and said companies should be subject to "common sense regulation" designed to protect communities. "Not all companies are doing it [building data centers] in the same way," she said. "Some are more responsible than others." Kaiser said responsible developments can use closed-loop water cooling systems and generate power independently rather than increasing demand on the existing electrical grid. Alpha Compute, she said, is pursuing projects designed to operate "off-grid, behind the meter," meaning the facilities would generate their own power rather than relying on electricity supplied through the local grid. Kaiser said that approach is intended to prevent the massive energy demands of data centers from straining existing infrastructure or contributing to higher electricity costs for nearby residents. ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY The company is developing a project in Pennsylvania, where Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments. Kaiser said Alpha Compute plans to comply with the regulations and welcomed provisions promoting cleaner energy. Pennsylvania is among a growing number of states confronting the rapid expansion of data centers. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott has pushed data centers to provide more of their own power and shoulder infrastructure costs as development accelerates across the state. Other governors have gone further. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM But she cautioned that policies that significantly restrict domestic development could have broader consequences for America's position in the global AI race. "Compute power has now become nearly a utility," Kaiser said, comparing the need for domestic computing infrastructure to energy independence. "We want to have the right to compute," she said. "We want to be able to process data within our own borders as a national security priority, but also for our own intellectual property to make sure we're not sending our data abroad." "We should have the right to both energy independence as well as compute power," she said, "so that Americans and American companies can process all of our sensitive data within our own borders."

articles.title: Jewish AG’s convention boycott exposes deepening Israel fault line among Michigan Democrats
articles.summary: Michigan Democrats hold their 2026 convention as Dana Nessel says she won't attend over antisemitism fears and pro-Palestinian activist clashes.
articles.body: LANSING, MI - Michigan Democrats gather Saturday in the battleground state's capital city to hold their 2026 state nominating convention amid controversy over recent antisemitic harassment and open hostility within the party over U.S. support for Israel. Democratic Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is Jewish, recently announced she wouldn't attend the confab due to security concerns, after anti-Israel party activists shouted down pro-Israel speakers, including Rep. Haley Stevens, at a prior convention in April. This weekend's convention comes as a growing number of Democrats push for cutting military aid to Israel, amidst the Israeli government's ongoing war against Hamas terrorists in Gaza. The convention is also being held just a few weeks after Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel who describes their military actions as "genocide," narrowly edged Stevens to win the Democratic Senate nomination for a crucial seat the Democrats must hold in the midterm elections. DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM "I don’t feel safe going. I feel like my presence isn’t going to be welcome. I don’t want to get chased around. I don’t want to get harassed. I don’t want to get yelled and screamed at. I don’t want to get booed off the stage, irrespective of what I’m saying," Nessel said during a roundtable discussion last month. "I believe that if I go, that is what will happen because it’s been happening to me." Responding, the Michigan Democratic Party said it is "committed to ensuring party-hosted events are safe and secure environments for all attendees." "We reject antisemitism, Islamophobia, and all forms of hateful conduct. We are working diligently with stakeholders, elected officials, and party membership to prepare for our August convention and look forward to welcoming Michigan Democrats to the Lansing Center on August 29," state party spokesperson Derrick Honeyman said in a statement. CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL IN MICHIGAN'S BLOCKBUSTER SENATE RACE Joan Lowenstein, endorsement chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, told Fox News Digital she hasn't "talked to anybody who thinks they will be unsafe at this convention." But Lowenstein, who also sits on the Michigan Democratic Party Central Committee, added, "Some people think it will be unpleasant and why should they bother." But other Jewish Democrats in Michigan are very concerned. "People are traumatized from the previous convention. Many people I talked to, many super progressive people, are really traumatized by the way they were treated, and the way Haley Stevens was booed, and the way other candidates were treated," Rabbi Asher Lopatin told Fox News Digital last week. Lopatin, who was interviewed after joining Republican Senate nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers at a campaign event to unveil Democrats supporting Rogers, referred to Nessel's decision not to attend the convention and said "it just shows how terrible these extremists are that they're intimidating even the attorney general of our state." WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW But Lopatin emphasized, "We got to be strong. We got to be proud. We got to be courageous. The Jewish community cannot cower." Stacy Gittleman, a lifelong Democrat who is supportive of Israel, attended the April convention. "I saw more Palestinian flags than American flags on the floor," Gittleman, a writer who published her observations at the convention on substack, told Fox News Digital this week. Gittleman said the jeers and what she highlighted as a "lack of decorum and disrespect" were signs to her of "how far left our party is drifting." The convention is being held as some Jewish leaders in Michigan are circulating an open letter urging Jewish Democrats and independents in the state to sign their names in support of Rogers. The news was first reported last week by the Jewish Insider and confirmed by Fox News Digital. "This is sort of a do-or-die moment," a person involved with the letter who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely told Fox News Digital. "There are many lifelong Democrats who are feeling homeless. ... It’s not just a leftward drift but has turned into an anti-Jewish drift as well." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Lowenstein, who doesn't support the petition, said those behind the letter "feel it’s an existential issue, and I think that represents a lot of people. And, so, they have to do what they have to do." "It’s sort of 50/50," she added. "Half the people I talk to say, ‘I could never vote for Abdul El-Sayed because of things he’s said about Israel and, consequentially, the Jewish community. And the other 50% say ‘it is so important for Jews as Americans to have an Democratic Senate that I could never vote for Mike Rogers.'" Rogers and El-Sayed are running to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The race is among a dozen that will determine if the Democrats win back the Senate majority from the GOP. Rogers, in an interview last week with Fox News Digital, reiterated that he's not asking Democratic voters to become Republicans. And he highlighted concerns he's heard from Democratic Jewish voters in Michigan. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE "I've talked to two young women who were at University of Michigan who were afraid to walk to class. They couldn't display their Star of David. To say that they're afraid is probably an understatement," he said. Rogers said "the violent rhetoric ... is going to make a difference" in the general election. El-Sayed is a former Wayne County Health Department director who, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. The epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018 has made support for Medicare for all a major component of his campaign and has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). But it's El-Sayed's stance and comments on Israel that have angered some Jewish people in Michigan, a state that also has a large Arab and Muslim population. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER El-Sayed used the word "bloodthirsty" to characterize Israel's military moves in Gaza in an MS NOW interview this month. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist. articles.title: Appeals court delivers unsettling ruling — and says Supreme Court left it no choice
articles.summary: A federal appeals court says Supreme Court precedent forced it to protect possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, raising urgent questions.
articles.body: A federal appeals court says decades-old Supreme Court precedent forced it to protect the in-home possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, as judges warned that rapidly advancing technology has complicated legal lines drawn nearly 25 years ago. The ruling exposes a widening gap between Supreme Court precedent and rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The Seventh Circuit said it was bound by a 2002 Supreme Court decision that rejected restrictions on sexually explicit depictions of fictional children when no actual child was involved in their creation. But two judges warned that modern AI can now generate images virtually indistinguishable from material depicting the abuse of real children. "Indeed, in Free Speech Coalition, the Supreme Court addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for virtual CSAM, but that was nearly twenty-five years ago, and the image-generation technology available today was likely unimaginable back then," Judge John Lee wrote. "Given the relentless advancement in artificial intelligence models, we have some concerns about the lines these cases draw, but we are not free to redraw them ourselves." WORKER AT SWANKY COUNTRY CLUB ACCUSED OF USING AI TO CREATE EXPLICIT PHOTOS OF TEEN: POLICE The Seventh Circuit affirmed a lower court’s dismissal of one of four charges against Steven Anderegg, who investigators said had hundreds of AI-generated sexually explicit images depicting children on devices seized from his Wisconsin home. Anderegg was charged with producing and distributing the AI-generated material, transferring it to a minor under 16, and possessing it. A federal district court dismissed only the possession charge on First Amendment grounds, leaving the other three charges intact. The Justice Department appealed that dismissal, arguing that the government should be permitted to prohibit possession of obscene virtual child sexual abuse material even when no actual child was involved in its creation. But the Seventh Circuit sided with the lower court. The government generally cannot criminalize the private possession of obscene material inside someone's home, but it can prohibit possession of child sexual abuse material involving real children because its creation exploits actual victims. However, the Supreme Court complicated that distinction in 2002 when it struck down restrictions covering sexually explicit images of fictional children created without using actual minors. The justices reasoned that the government's overriding interest in protecting children from exploitation did not apply in the same way when no real child was involved. AOC OFFERS RARE PRAISE TO LATE SEN GRAHAM FOR BACKING AI PORN BILL NOW STALLED IN HOUSE Hans von Spakovsky, a senior fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital that the appeals court "had no choice but to uphold the dismissal under the First Amendment" because of the Supreme Court's ruling. But von Spakovsky agreed with the concurrence by Lee and Judge Joshua Kolar, who warned the Supreme Court that the rapid growth of AI technology could require the justices to revisit precedent. "Unforunately, AI-generated images are now virtualy indistinguishable from the real thing and some of these images be created based on real child sexual abuse material," von Spavosky said. "Technology may have overtaken and overwhelmed the reasoning used in those prior decisions." NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS The Supreme Court previously ruled in Free Speech Coalition that taking images of real children and "morphing" them into sexually explicit poses would not be protected under its ruling on the possession of child sexual abuse material depicting fictional children because the practice involves the interests of real children. Justice Department lawyers have warned that the rise of AI-generated child sexual abuse material could bog down investigators trying to identify real victims, as increasingly realistic artificial images become harder to distinguish from depictions of actual abuse. HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM Judges Lee and Kolar raised another concern in their concurrence, citing research that found hundreds of child sexual abuse material images in a major dataset used to train image-generating AI. The judges suggested that could create a link between AI-generated material and the exploitation of real children, though they stressed that the government did not raise the issue in this case and that the record was insufficient to resolve it. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Justice Clarence Thomas anticipated the dilemma more than two decades ago, warning in the Supreme Court’s 2002 ruling that advancing technology could eventually make virtual depictions indistinguishable from child sexual abuse material involving real victims. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If technological advances thwart prosecution of ‘unlawful speech,’ the Government may well have a compelling interest in barring or otherwise regulating some narrow category of ‘lawful speech’" to enforce laws against material produced through the abuse of real children, Thomas wrote.

articles.title: GOV JEFF LANDRY: SpaceX bets on Louisiana as America’s next frontier takes off in the South
articles.summary: Louisiana's governor says SpaceX's decision confirms the state's momentum after tax cuts, workforce training, and $250 billion in investments.
articles.body: For generations, Americans looked west when they thought about opportunity. Today, they should look south. Louisiana has always powered America. We fueled the nation with energy, fed it through our farms and ports, built ships that defended it, and manufactured the products that helped it grow. Now, we are helping lead America’s next frontier: space. NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND—OR CHINA WILL With SpaceX choosing Louisiana for its newest chapter, our state is taking its place at the center of the economic and technological race that will define the 21st century. HOW AMERICAN ENERGY HELPED BUILD 250 YEARS OF FREEDOM AND OPPORTUNITY Together, these projects are creating thousands of jobs, strengthening American energy security, and cementing Louisiana’s role as a global energy leader. Louisiana is not betting its future on a single industry. We are building an economy that leads in energy, manufacturing, technology, and now aerospace. INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE SpaceX is the latest chapter in that story. Some will see rockets. I see what they make possible. ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM I see high-paying jobs for Louisiana workers. I see engineers, welders, electricians, fabricators, software developers, and skilled tradespeople building the future right here. I see students who once believed they had to leave Louisiana to pursue careers in technology and innovation realizing they can build those careers at home. I see communities gaining investment, growth, and optimism. Most importantly, I see Louisiana becoming a state that attracts talent instead of exporting it. That matters because the greatest challenge facing our state has never been a lack of resources. It has been a lack of opportunity. For decades, Louisiana was known for what we were losing. Today, we are becoming known for what we are gaining. The proof is already visible. Louisiana recently recorded population growth for the second consecutive year. Young adults accounted for most of that growth. Our labor force participation rate recorded one of the largest increases in America as thousands more Louisianians entered or reentered the workforce. People are choosing Louisiana again. SpaceX did not create that momentum. It confirms it. This project joins a growing list of investments that send the same message to the country and the world: Louisiana is open for business, ready to compete, and prepared to win. For too long, Louisiana was told to think smaller. We were told the industries of the future belonged somewhere else. SpaceX proves otherwise. That should make every Louisianian proud. More importantly, it should make every American optimistic. Because when companies choose to build in Louisiana, they are choosing to build in America. The future of American energy, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, and now space exploration is being written in places willing to compete for it. Louisiana is competing. articles.title: Trump’s tougher round-two birthright citizenship strategy hinges on key legal distinction, experts say
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's new birthright citizenship orders target children of terrorists and foreign government employees using classic legal exceptions.
articles.body: Conservative legal experts say President Donald Trump’s latest attempts to narrow birthright citizenship and crack down on birth tourism may have stronger legal footing than his first effort. After the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in June that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment, Trump issued two new executive orders taking narrower approaches to citizenship and birth tourism. The first, signed Aug. 6, directs federal agencies to withhold documents recognizing citizenship from certain children born when neither parent is a U.S. citizen, including some whose parents are members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, foreign-government employees or participants in transactions or fraud intended to obtain birthright citizenship. Experts from the Manhattan Institute, America First Legal and the America First Policy Institute, all right-of-center organizations, argued that Trump’s new order is narrower than his first and is built around longstanding exceptions to birthright citizenship that they believe could apply here. TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK "The Supreme Court has long recognized that there are exceptions to the 14th Amendment's birthright citizenship clause for the aliens who are considered children of invading armies or the children of ambassadors," America First Policy Institute senior fellow Chad Mizelle, who previously served as the Justice Department’s chief of staff, told Fox News Digital. "So in a situation where you have a terrorist here contrary to the laws of the United States … who is looking to do harm … That has long been recognized by the Supreme Court, and basically going back to the history of our country, as recognized exceptions to any sort of claim of birthright citizenship." United States v. Wong Kim Ark, decided by the Supreme Court in 1898, recognized exceptions to birthright citizenship for children of diplomats and children of alien enemies born during a hostile occupation. Trump’s order argues that members of foreign terrorist organizations can fall within that enemy exception. TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP FIGHT COMES ROARING BACK WITH ‘INVADERS’ PLAY AFTER KAVANAUGH ROADMAP "The Supreme Court ruled that you can't restrict birthright citizenship to kids of people in the country temporarily or illegally," Manhattan Institute director of constitutional studies Ilya Shapiro told Fox News Digital. "But what the new executive order does is it goes to one of the classic exceptions to birthrights citizenship, two of the classic exceptions, those who owe an allegiance to a foreign government, meaning employed by a foreign governing diplomats otherwise, and those who are invaders of foreign armies and terrorists, members of foreign organizations hostile to America, certainly qualify in that category." David Bier, the director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, however, argued that the president’s attempt to redefine what constitutes an alien enemy without going through Congress puts the administration on legally shaky ground. "Congress ultimately establishes what it means to be subject to U.S. jurisdiction," Bier told Fox News Digital. "There's this very limited exception for accredited diplomats and everyone else in the United States is subject to U.S. laws so the idea that the president himself on his own authority can decide who is subject U. S. jurisdiction and U.S. laws is really a radical expansion and assertion of executive power and really would be unprecedented in the history of the United States." JACKSON ACCUSES THOMAS OF ECHOING INFAMOUSLY RACIST COURT DECISION IN BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CLASH "I really do think this case is testing a different proposition from the earlier case," Bier added, explaining that the issue at hand has more to do with executive power than birthright citizenship. "And I think it's a lot more questionable as well." Amanda Frost, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, pointed out that United States v. Wong Kim Ark specifies that only children of enemies "occupying" some portion of the country are barred from citizenship at birth, meaning that Trump’s order would not apply to terrorists simply residing within the country. She said the Trump administration could potentially expand who is legally defined as a diplomat to preclude more people from birthright citizenship, but explained such a move would make it difficult to prosecute individuals for criminal offenses, a concern shared by Bier. Frost and Bier both believe the new executive order should be ruled unconstitutional. Some have floated the issue of standing as a potential problem for those looking to challenge Trump's order. Legal standing requires plaintiffs to show they suffered or imminently face a concrete injury caused by the defendant that a court can remedy. "It's going to be interesting to see who actually does have standing to challenge this order," America First Legal co-founder and president Gene Hamilton told Fox News Digital. "Is there somebody who thinks that they're going to swept up in the definition of a foreign terrorist organization? And if so, it would be kind of fun to see them try to sue the government or have someone sue on their behalf." Trump’s new order is already facing legal resistance. TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION' The same groups who challenged his initial order are now arguing that his new one unlawfully creates exceptions to birthright citizenship that conflict with the Supreme Court’s June ruling. The order remains on the books but is not scheduled to take effect until Sept. 6, with a Maryland judge scheduled to hear an injunction request Aug. 28 and a related motion still pending in New Hampshire. Issued on the same day as the first new executive order, the second order directed the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to deny travel visas to or pursue removal actions against individuals believed to be in the country for the purposes of birth tourism. Birth tourism is a process through which noncitizens enter the United States while pregnant and give birth in order to secure citizenship for their child. Hamilton described this second order as being on "sound, solid legal footing." "It relies and invokes Section 215(a) of the INA to impose conditions and delegates authority of the Secretary of State … to ensure that we are not granting visas and allowing people to remain on visas who may be engaged in birth tourism," he explained. "It is the sovereign right and province of all governments across the world, and certainly the United States is no different, to determine who should be able to receive a visa and who shouldn't. There's no entitlement to a visa. There's no constitutional right to a visa." SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS Critics also argue that the administration already had tools to combat birth tourism. Since 2020, State Department rules have directed consular officers to deny visitor visas when they have reason to believe an applicant’s primary purpose is traveling to the United States to give birth and obtain citizenship for the child. "No new executive orders are required for the federal government to go after birth tourism operators or deny fraudulent visa applications," Center for American Progress senior director of immigration policy Debu Gandhi told Fox News Digital. "Americans should take note that from day one, the Trump administration has tried to evade the Constitution's clear and unequivocal language on citizenship and unilaterally decide who is born an American." If the administration’s latest effort fails, supporters of further limits on birthright citizenship could turn to Congress or pursue a constitutional amendment, which would require approval by three-fourths of the states. Shapiro says that the administration is on "solid ground" but noted that "if they had proceeded originally in this more targeted, narrower way" then the Supreme Court may not have ruled against them originally. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

articles.title: Viral Dearborn pastor delivers blunt warning on El-Sayed Senate bid: ‘Can you imagine?’
articles.summary: Pastor Lorenzo Sewell warns that Abdul El-Sayed could recommend federal judges aligned with Sharia law if elected to the Michigan Senate seat.
articles.body: DETROIT — A Black Christian pastor who went viral online for clashing with the city council in the nearby majority-Arab city of Dearborn issued a stark warning about Michigan senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. "Can you imagine him being in the Senate, being able to recommend federal judges to presidents?" Pastor Lorenzo Sewell of 180 Church said during an interview with Fox News Digital. "That's his goal. His goal is to be able to recommend federal judge to presidents for appointments, and then we're going to find ourselves in Sharia law all over this land." The Democratic nominee for Senate in the Wolverine State said in a 2009 New York Times interview that he was following Sharia law when he took out a special type of loan for an Ann Arbor condo. Sharia Law typically prevents interest on loans, and in some cases, Sharia-compliant Muslims can obtain loans wherein the amount of interest that would be paid over time is instead added to the purchase price of the home. VANCE UNLOADS ON EL-SAYED OVER SHARIA REMARKS: ‘THAT’S NOT MY GRANDPA’S DEMOCRATIC PARTY’ "Ultimately, the question is, when I die and I stand before God and go through everything I did in my life, I don’t want to say I did it the easy way instead of the Shariah-compliant way," El-Sayed told the Times. El-Sayed's spokeswoman Roxie Richner told the Washington Free Beacon when the report resurfaced earlier this month that, "While he lives by the rules of his faith, as many Americans of various faiths do, Abdul opposes any effort by any religious community to write their faith laws into the laws of our country." In a response to Fox News Digital, Richner characterized Sewell's comments as "cheap attacks and hateful rhetoric" from an ally of El-Sayed's Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. EL-SAYED'S AGENDA PUTS ‘PERMANENTLY’ CHANGED AMERICA ON THE LINE IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE, GOP FIREBRAND WARNS As referenced by Sewell, members of the Senate often recommend political appointees to presidents, and ultimately, in the case of federal courts, the Senate confirms them. He called El-Sayed a ‘fake doctor,’ referencing criticism of how El-Sayed has described his medical credentials. El-Sayed earned an M.D. from Columbia University but did not complete a residency and has not held a medical license in Michigan or New York. Sewell also accused prominent Muslim politicians including, El-Sayed, of resisting assimilation into American culture. "This is the type of conquering religion whereby people like Abdul El-Sayed, people like [Rep.] Rashida Tlaib, you have [Rep. Ilhan] Omar over there in Minnesota — you look at these people that have a desire, not to assimilate to our culture, but to take over our culture," said Sewell. "They will wave flags to say 'free Palestine.' They will say 'to the river, to the sea,' all on American soil. I mean, these are the type of people that are not looking to assimilate. They're looking to conquer." He added that if Christian ministers and "patriots" didn't step up to combat Sharia law, he would be, "preaching out the Quran" and his "church would become a mosque." The pastor, who was born and raised on the east side of Detroit and says he was a "student of the streets" and "mentored by murderers," is no stranger to media attention. TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY Just last week, he was the subject of a viral video from a Dearborn, Michigan, city council meeting. "We are not a nation of Muslims, we are nation of Christians!" he said in an impassioned speech directed towards the councilors. "America, we have lost this city. This is a city that is no longer up under American laws; we are up under Sharia law. We will not have it anymore." DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN He also hosted then-candidate Donald Trump at his church during Trump's 2024 campaign, rallying Black voters. He spoke at the RNC that year, too. Throughout the interview with Fox News Digital, Sewell expressed disdain for Democratic Party politicians, who he says have long oppressed African Americans. Sewell isn't a fan of the company El-Sayed keeps, either. He slammed El-Sayed for campaigning with socialist streamer Hasan Piker, who said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." Piker has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, and said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and spewed a litany of antisemitic comments. "I believe that there's treason for you to say those type of words, that America deserves 9/11," said Sewell. He described Piker, who last week mocked the death of Charlie Kirk by singing a viral internet song in front of a crowd of socialists, as the "demonic" version of Kirk. HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA El-Sayed further distanced himself from Piker Monday after Piker argued on his Twitch show that rhetoric linking American Jews closely to Israel could ultimately provoke attacks against American Jews — comments critics condemned as antisemitic victim-blaming. articles.title: Seneca Nation requests reversal on ‘Lake America’ executive order
articles.summary: Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca called Friday for President Trump to rescind his order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” citing a 225-year-old treaty between Native Americans and the U.S. government. Seneca said in a statement that this name change, which President Trump authorized in a Thursday executive order, violated the terms of…
articles.body:
Seneca Nation President J. Conrad Seneca called Friday for President Trump to rescind his order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” citing a 225-year-old treaty between Native Americans and the U.S. government.

Seneca said in a statement that this name change, which President Trump authorized in a Thursday executive order , violated the terms of the 1794 Treaty of Canandaigua .

“The President cannot assert ownership over our culture or erase it through irresponsible political action,” he said in a statement.

President George Washington and leaders of the Haudenosaunee confederacy, which includes the Seneca Nation, signed the treaty to assert a shared commitment to peace. The document laid out the Seneca Nation’s boundaries as “beginning on Lake Ontario.”

The lake’s name comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” which translates to “lake of shining waters.” In the traditional Seneca language, the body of water is called “sga:nyodai:yoh,” which means “beautiful lake,” according to the nation’s president.

Trump made the decision to change the lake’s name this week amid an escalating trade fight with Canada. Last year, the president also signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.”

“If you think about it, we have a gulf, now we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean,” Trump quipped to reporters in the Oval Office during Thursday’s signing ceremony. “Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D), whose state borders the lake, said she would not honor the renaming request.

Additionally, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the lake’s ties to Native American heritage in a statement condemning its renaming on Thursday.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote on the social platform X .

The leader added that “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

articles.title: When bureaucracy kills: When will our government act to keep women safe?
articles.summary: Women are 17 percent more likely to be killed than men in car accidents, and 73 percent more likely to be seriously injured.
articles.body:
In 2019, my family suffered a head-on collision with a wrong-way driver, when he tried to pass a motorcycle up a hill and smashed his Ford F-150 truck head-on into our car. The crash left my husband and son with a few broken bones, while my daughter and I were gravely injured.

Our seatbelts tore through our abdomens and into our internal organs. My head slammed into my airbag with enough force to cause a traumatic brain injury. Why had my son and husband been protected by their seatbelts and airbags while the same safety devices almost killed me and my daughter?

Soon after the car crash, a story from Consumer Reports sent me on a journey to better understand what had happened. I discovered our injuries weren’t random: women are 17 percent more likely to be killed than men, and 73 percent more likely to be seriously injured .

At the time, I worked for a think tank advocating the use of data and design to solve public problems, a practice we called “public interest technology.” I earned a living telling people the government was capable of solving hard problems, so I assumed, given my connections, I could help save women’s lives. Especially because a well-engineered solution already existed.

There is a company builds “biofidelic” crash test dummies. At the facility, a display case illustrates the evolution of crash test dummies since the 1950s. The earliest female dummy had pointy breasts, a wig and lipstick. Otherwise, it was simply a scaled-down version of a male dummy.

But its latest model accurately represents 95 percent of the female population. Biofidelic dummies account for the anatomical differences between men and women that matter in car safety design.

Men have stronger neck musculature, which prevents brain injuries when their heads hit airbags. Men tend to be taller and broader, so they sit in the purportedly correct position for safety technologies. Women, in contrast, are considered “out of position” drivers.

Seatbelts sit across men’s hip bones, rather than slicing into their internal organs. Men’s necks are protected from whiplash because they reach headrests at the right spot. And the spacing of women’s spinal columns are different, which explained my spinal fractures.

Until 2011, female dummies were not required in crash tests. Today, no American car manufacturer uses biofidelic female dummies, because they can obtain a five-star crash test rating without them.

I emailed the chief data officer in the Biden White House after learning about this issue. We had worked together at the same think tank, so I thought she would be shocked to hear about a data problem that was killing women. Unfortunately, that administration was bogged down in a sea of ideological commitments guided by political expediency, pursued at the expense of common sense and public safety.

I tried to explain that if the car industry did not address its longstanding car crash safety bias before the doomed electric vehicle rollout my former co-worker was assigned to, more electric vehicles on the road would mean more female fatalities. Former President Joe Biden lost a wife and young daughter to a car crash . I thought that surely this issue would grab the White House’s attention.

But it did not. My acquaintance was not going to tell Biden to halt his big EV project, even if it meant saving lives. First she would save the environment, then she would get around to women eventually. Sadly, 44,000 women would die over the course of her term.

Next, I met with several high-ranking Department of Transportation officials, including the deputy head of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which awards crash test safety ratings. The agency’s dummies are modeled on the standard size American 1970s-era American male . Their female dummy represents only 5 percent of women.

Anyone who deviates from that standard — Americans who are taller, shorter, heavier, lighter, female or pregnant — well, you’re on your own if you get into a crash.

Worse, the federal agency does not mandate testing with a female dummy in the driver’s seat. Surely, this was an oversight, or else the five-star crash test safety rating was a bald-faced lie.

Department of Transportation officials listened as I presented my data. Then they shared their own data demonstrating that women weren’t injured or killed at a rate higher than men, if you assumed men were “normal” drivers and women were an aberration.

“Why don’t you mandate tests with women in the driver’s seat?” I asked. Their reply: “We can’t mandate every test.”

They were doing great things with automatic braking, they added, which was saving lives left and right. I ran my hand over the scar that bisects my torso, which automatic breaking had failed to prevent.

How did the department decide testing with women in the driver’s seat was too expensive, but that investing in automatic breaking was the way forward? How did they decide who should live and who should die?

Last November, the Trump Transportation Department issued a press release advocating for the use of biofidelic dummies. Finally.

If the administration really wants to change the regulations, it should mandate their use rather than simply acknowledging their existence. But hey, progress is progress. And the bipartisan She DRIVES Act , sponsored by nine congresswomen and five congressmen, has been introduced into the last two congressional calendars.

No one’s family is supposed to get hit by a wrong-way driver on a sunny day in the U.S. When the government learns that thousands of women die each year because they have been looking at the data wrong, bureaucrats are supposed to say, “thank you for bringing this to our attention — we’ll get right on a solution.” Instead, they dissemble.

I no longer trust the government to act in my best interest or to prioritize my health and wellbeing. Is this the America that was once the crown jewel in the pantheon of innovation?

Today, U.S. road deaths per 10,000 drivers rank just slightly above India . Drivers in Mexico and Sierra Leone are less likely to die on the road than drivers in Ohio. Is it any mystery why this is the case?

Hana Schank is a journalist, technologist and policy strategist. Previously she worked in the Obama White House as a digital expert, and ran the Public Interest Technology team at New America .

articles.body:
Tom Begich, a Democrat running for governor in Alaska, announced Friday evening he was dropping out of the race.

The former state senator endorsed his Democratic opponent, former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. Both candidates advanced to the general election in Alaska’s open primary earlier this month.

In a video shared on the social platform X announcing his campaign’s suspension, Begich cited funding concerns, saying that keeping the campaign going through the November election “would take millions more than we have.”

“We’ve spoken with the other leading Democrat in this race. He shared data, and we’ve reviewed our own internal information, and the data we’ve seen makes clear that the strongest path to winning in November is not two democratic candidates competing for the same donors and resources; it’s bringing those people together behind one ticket,” Begich said.

Julia Hnilicka, a candidate for lieutenant governor running with Begich, said Kreiss-Tomkins “shares our commitment” to issues like school funding, energy affordability and housing access.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates Alaska’s gubernatorial race to replace Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) as “likely Republican.”

Kreiss-Tomkins led the pack in Alaska’s open primary race earlier this month with nearly 23 percent of the vote, according to Decision Desk HQ. Begich received just under 21 percent, and Republican candidate Bernadette Wilson garnered 10 percent.

Wilson and Kreiss-Tomkins will face off in the general election this November.

Former Alaskan Gov. Tony Knowles (D) has backed Kreiss-Tomkins in this race. The Democrat is running to expand Medicaid coverage, bring down energy costs, fund public education and expand affordable housing options in the state.

The former state representative also supports a moratorium on all new data centers in the state until Alaska’s legislature passes “comprehensive regulation” for these projects, according to his campaign website .

Wilson has campaigned on a platform to eliminate income-based inequality in education, promote the state’s oil and gas industries and partner with President Trump. The state has voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections.

“The incoming governor has the opportunity to partner with the president to make sure that we take these first two years of what will be hopefully our administration and the last couple [years] of the president’s administration and really make a big impact on the country,” she told Newsmax earlier this month.

“So the goal is to make sure that … when people look back and they reflect back on Donald Trump’s time as president, that they reflect back fondly to Alaska and what we accomplished in oil and gas,” Wilson continued.

articles.title: Judge Talwani and why liberal complaints about the ‘shadow docket’ are so hollow
articles.summary: Litigants have been accused of forum shopping. Here’s what that means.
articles.body:
This week, the Trump administration found itself in a familiar position: facing an injunction from Judge Indira Talwani of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. Indeed, it had just secured an order from the Supreme Court on its emergency docket lifting her earlier injunction on the U.S. Postal Service requiring voting lists to confirm U.S. citizenship.

The case against the executive order on mail-in ballots has reasonable arguments on both sides, although (as I have said previously) the challengers are likely to prevail in defeating the rule or at least delaying the policy until after the midterm elections. The Constitution gives states the primary responsibility over “the times, places, and manner of holding elections.”

However, the U.S. Postal Service is a federal agency, and the federal government does have a role in the funding and regulation of federal elections. More importantly, the Trump administration is arguing that it is not barring mail-in voting but merely imposing “modest informational requirements.” Non-citizens cannot vote in federal elections, and the new rule “does not displace a single state election law. And it need not and should not prevent a single voter from voting by mail.”

The controversy over Talwani is not necessarily the merits of her decision that the rule convenes the constitutional framework. Indeed, the Supreme Court did not rule on the merits and could well rule in favor of her interpretation. The controversy is the pattern of sweeping injunctions by Talwani and a few other judges.

Litigants have been accused of forum-shopping by going to liberal, Democratically appointed judges to prevent Trump policies from being implemented in a wide array of areas, including immigration, elections, reduction in government bureaucracies, and foreign aid.

Like her colleague in Boston, U.S. District Court Judge Brian Murphy , Talwani is viewed by many as a one-stop-shop judge for forum-shopping. Both have issued hair-trigger injunctions, and both have been repeatedly reversed.

Talwani was reversed on Aug. 24 for imposing an injunction against the mail-in balloting policy. Her injunction was taken to be premature and without a legal injury, since the administration had not issued a formal rule. The truth is, the challengers had her at hello. She did not wait for a showing of a cognizable injury before issuing another injunction, because the decision appeared made before the case hit her own docket.

Previously, Talwani showed the same inclination in other cases. For example, she issued an injunction against revoking the humanitarian parole program for hundreds of thousands of immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua and Venezuela. Her order was lifted on appeal.

She also issued an injunction to stop the Trump Administration from defunding Planned Parenthood. That order was also set aside on appeal.

Regardless of the outcome of this latest injunction, Talwani has offered the strongest case in favor of the expanded use of the emergency docket, also known as the “shadow docket.” Liberal law professors and litigants have bewailed the expanded use of this docket at the Supreme Court to resolve cases without the need for a long briefing and oral argument. However, judges like Talwani have created legitimate concerns of the gaming of the system to harness or freeze new policies. This is why the “shadow docket” has become more prominent.

This year, confidential memoranda were leaked from the court on the use of the emergency docket and published by the New York Times. It was only the latest such strategic leak from a court that was once the paragon of confidentiality and civility.

The internal exchanges of the justices were illuminating as to the majority’s underlying reason for allowing this fast-track review. The immediate issue was a move by the Environmental Protection Agency to impose unlawful regulatory burdens on electric utilities despite a countervailing earlier ruling in Michigan v. EPA. Chief Justice Roberts believed (as did many) that the EPA was using the ongoing litigation to force utilities to spend billions of dollars to comply with new regulations that the Supreme Court had already rejected.

“In other words,” Roberts wrote, “the absence of stay allowed the agency to effectively implement an important program we held to be contrary to law.”

As with the national injunctions that plagued the Trump administration in its first year, this tactic was all too familiar. Litigants would go to liberal judges in Washington, Boston, and other blue cities to secure injunctions that would take years to fully litigate. That approach effectively allowed individual judges to pursue their own preferred policies or to prevent a president from carrying out promises made during an election. At most, the president might have a year left after these cases slogged through the conventional appellate process. It is an administrative version of the old adage that “justice delayed is justice denied.”

What concerned the justices was that many of these injunctions directly contravened earlier precedent, exposing the cynical purpose of these orders. For a president to be able to carry out major changes, he had to run a gauntlet of hundreds of judges, any one of whom could effectively negate reforms. In response, the Supreme Court ramped up the use of the emergency docket and cracked down on national injunctions, quickly reversing the rapidly increasing number of injunctions against the Trump administration.

With the midterm elections rapidly approaching, the odds favor challengers in either running out the clock or prevailing on the merits on the mail-in ballots. But Talwani and some other judges have reinforced suspicions of the Roberts court that some courts are willing allies of partisan groups in seeking to gum up the system.

Ironically, Roberts is one of the most likely conservative justices to be concerned with the Trump administration’s effort to force election integrity reforms on the states. Either way, it is the shadow of these judges, not the docket, that is casting the most ominous concern for many of the Supreme Court justices.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution . “

articles.title: Large quantities of khat are being intercepted at US airports. What is it?
articles.summary: Khat is listed as Schedule I drug in the United states. Where is it coming from?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has intercepted thousands of pounds of khat at U.S. airports over just the last month — with much of it coming with smugglers on passenger planes.

“Our officers do an outstanding job stopping shipments like these,” Michael Pfeiffer, the acting director of operations at CBP’s Chicago Field Office, said last week after the seizure of almost 1,200 pounds of khat that reportedly arrived at O’Hare International Airport with three travelers from Senegal.

“Criminals keep trying different ways to sneak their contraband into the United States and our officers do a better job of finding it and pursuing prosecutorial options,” Pfeiffer added.

In addition to the interceptions at O’Hare, CBP officials at Baltimore Washington International seized a total of just under 1,260 pounds of khat in mid-August, much of which was found in suitcases belonging to two New York men who arrived from London. Large quantities of khat were also seized at nearby Washington Dulles International Airport this month, first after a New Yorker arriving from Paris attempted to smuggle in 367 pounds, and later when two men from Georgia and New York were found with a total of 764 pounds after arriving from Casablanca and Paris, respectively.

While some (not all) CBP offices say they’re seeing an uptick in khat smugglers attempting to bring their contraband by passenger plane, the illegal trafficking of khat into the U.S. — usually in cargo shipments — is not a new phenomenon.

Khat, pronounced like “cot,” is the name for a shrub (Catha edulis) usually grown in parts of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, but it’s also the common name for the leaves the shrub produces, which can be chewed for their stimulant-like properties. Khat users often store the leaves in their cheeks, kind of like tobacco, and chew to release its main active stimulant, an alkaloid known as cathinone. Cathinone is chemically similar to amphetamines and produces “excitement, loss of appetite, and euphoria,” a review published in the Qatar Medical Journal explains. Researchers say, however, that the stimulant effects produced by khat are significantly milder than amphetamines.

Because of its cathinone content, khat categorized as a Schedule I drug in the United States, meaning it has “no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse,” according to the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

Khat users may also experience “grandiose delusions, paranoia, nightmares, hallucinations, and hyperactivity,” the agency says, as well as potential long-term effects of liver damage, suicidal depression, heart complications and violent tendencies, among others.

Despite this, its use is not regulated in parts of the world, especially in places where it’s cultivated for social use. Yemen, for example, uses a significant amount of its water supply (some estimates say has high as 40%) which is legal and widely consumed for recreational purposes.

Being a lucrative crop, its also among the substances often trafficked into the United States. The street value of the 1,172 pounds seized in Chicago this month was said to be worth more than $140,000, or around $120 per pound, according to CBP’s news release.

Government records show it’s regularly seized at customs and border stops, with officers intercepting around 19,000 pounds so far in 2026. (Of the last several years, CBP officers seized the most khat in 2023, at 70,044 pounds.)

A CBP spokesperson, in a statement to Nexstar, said the agency has “consistently interdicted its illegal importation for decades.”

“It is not a new trend; rather, it remains a persistent enforcement focus as officers continue to intercept shipments and travelers attempting to smuggle this stimulant into the U.S.,” the CBP said.

articles.title: White House teleprompter operator who placed bets on Trump’s speeches ordered to pay $172K
articles.summary: The White House teleprompter operator who placed online bets on President Trump’s speeches has been ordered to pay a total of $172,000, a federal agency said Friday. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) said in a news release that Gabriel Perez must pay out his profits from trade, totaling $107,539.02, in addition to a civil…
articles.body:
The White House teleprompter operator who placed online bets on President Trump’s speeches has been ordered to pay a total of $172,000, a federal agency said Friday.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) said in a news release that Gabriel Perez must pay out his profits from trade, totaling $107,539.02, in addition to a civil monetary penalty of $65,000.

The White House suspended Perez from his role last month after online prediction market platform Kalshi flagged suspicious trades to federal regulators linked to the teleprompter operator.

A White House official confirmed to The Hill at the end of July that Perez was no longer employed in the federal government.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said last month the president was informed of the situation and “believes it is deeply unfortunate and, frankly, a disgrace.” Perez had worked for the president since 2016.

Perez is accused of using his knowledge of the content of Trump’s speeches to make trades in presidential mention markets, generating over $100,000 from these bets between December 2025 and February 2026.

Mention markets allow users to place bets on whether someone will say a specific word or phrase, such as country names, general political topics or campaign phrases.

The CFTC said Perez has been banned from making trades on prediction markets for three years.

Robert DeNault, the head of enforcement and legal counsel at Kalshi, responded to the CFTC’s penalties in a statement on Friday evening.

“It doesn’t matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences,” DeNault wrote on social media .

Prediction markets have come under heightened scrutiny in the past year over insider trading concerns.

In April, a U.S. Army soldier was charged for using his knowledge of the top-secret operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to place bets on Polymarket. He allegedly made a profit of over $400,000 on these trades.

Kalshi and Polymarket have introduced new guardrails this year to crack down on insider trading on their platforms. Kalshi now prevents politicians, athletes and other groups from placing bets in certain markets. Polymarket updated its rules to make clear that it bans trades based on confidential information.
