articles.title: NOAA, almanacs release fall weather predictions: What could it be like near you?
articles.summary: Cold and wet, hot and dry – what’s in store for you may depend on the forecast you look at.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Believe it or not, fall will be upon us soon, with the autumnal equinox less than a month away.

While it’s too early to say exactly how much of that perfect fall weather you’ll get to experience, there are forecasts that have attempted to offer some insight. We’re not talking about just the almanac predictions , either. Last week, NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center released its long-range forecast for September, October, and November.

The three forecasts, however, don’t necessarily agree.

Last month, the Old Farmer’s Almanac put out its fall forecast, predicting a “warmer than average” fall, with a “cool, wet” outlook in the Pacific Northwest and northern New England. Much of the Plains and Rocky Mountains could see a warm and dry fall, as could some states in the central Gulf region, while the Midwest, Ohio Valley and the East Coast may experience a cool and dry fall.

The Farmers’ Almanac, meanwhile, is calling for almost the exact opposite, suggesting we’re in for a “dramatic drench.”

The Pacific Northwest is the only region that is forecasted to stay dry, while the neighboring states could see “below-average rainfall,” the Almanac predicts. States primarily in the northern two-thirds of the country will be cold through fall as the rest stay warm. The central portion of the U.S., as well as New England, could be “wet,” the Midwest may be “rainy,” and the Southeast is predicted to be “stormy.”

Both publications claim to be 80% accurate with their long-range forecasts, which are fueled by their own secret formulas, though research shows only about half of the forecasts produced by the Farmers’ Almanac were correct.

“There are those who believe [them] and those who don’t,” meteorologist Rich Segal, who recently retired from Nexstar’s KXAN, previously explained. “It’s more like a crapshoot of trusting something that far into the future since there are times the forecast is blown in the first 24 hours.”

Warmer-than-average, plus El Niño’s impact

Where the almanacs are calling for cooler weather, NOAA suggests temperatures could be above-average. In areas where the almanacs suggest it will be wet, NOAA’s forecast offers a murkier outlook.

The long-range forecast shows all but a few states leaning toward hotter-than-normal temperatures between September and November. The Pacific Northwest is most likely to see above-average weather. A handful of states, those shown in white on the map below, have about equal chances of seeing a warm fall, a cool fall and an average fall.

Several states also find themselves in a toss-up situation when it comes to precipitation.

The Southwest and Southeast are more likely to see above-average rain, while the Northeast and Pacific Northwest are more likely to be dry. The forecast isn’t very clear for everyone else. Most states have equal chances of below-average, above-average or average precipitation between now and November.

Hawaii, which isn’t shown on the maps above, has a different outlook. Oahu, Maui, Kauai and the Big Island are most likely to see above-normal temperatures this fall, before shifting to a cooler winter season in early 2027. Below-normal precipitation is increasingly likely for all of Hawaii starting in October, the Climate Prediction Center said.

The early signs of El Niño — which forecasters believe will reach the highest strength level this year — are appearing in the fall forecasts above. That’s especially true for the Pacific Northwest, which could be warm and dry, and in the South, where wetter conditions are expected. Other impacts of El Niño on fall weather include suppressing hurricane activity in the Atlantic and contributing to more high-tide flooding on the West Coast.

Even NOAA’s outlooks are subject to change. If they were released any earlier, their reliability would likely decline, Jon Gottschalck, Operational Prediction Branch Chief at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, previously told Nexstar.

articles.title: Abbott bars Texas agencies from funding Flock cameras
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) ordered all state agencies this week to halt funding for Flock cameras amid growing concerns nationwide about the misuse of the roadside camera network. The decision, which was communicated to state agencies on Thursday evening, came as The Texas Tribune said it was preparing to publish an investigation into the…
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) ordered all state agencies this week to halt funding for Flock cameras amid growing concerns nationwide about the misuse of the roadside camera network.

The decision, which was communicated to state agencies on Thursday evening, came as The Texas Tribune said it was preparing to publish an investigation into the state’s funding of these cameras. The newsroom reported that the Texas legislature authorized a 2023 hike in auto insurance costs to purchase and maintain 3,200 Flock cameras across the state.

Abbott’s press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, noted in a statement shared with The Hill on Saturday that nearly all Flock cameras in the state are purchased by cities through federal funding.

“To the extent any funding comes from Texas agencies, those agencies are clarifying that those funds cannot be used for Flock cameras,” Mahaleris said.

A spokesperson for Flock emphasized in a statement to The Hill Saturday that the company’s technology is “an important public safety tool” for Texas law enforcement agencies.

“We support thoughtful legislation and strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails that ensure technology is used responsibly while preserving law enforcement’s ability to use effective tools to keep people safe,” the Flock spokesperson said.

Abbott’s decision comes as a growing number of cities cancel their contracts with Flock over reported abuse of the company’s expansive roadside camera network. In Lufkin, Texas, a city police officer was indicted in April on 100 counts of misusing Flock data.

The city of Tempe, Ariz., canceled its police department’s $80,000 contract with the company this week over a growing concern about abuse of data across the nation.

Tempe Mayor Corey Woods told NewsNation’s Blake Burman Thursday evening that “the potential for misuse was too great.”

“In order to make sure that we’re not only just being directly upfront with our residents, our main goal was to provide public safety, but also make sure that we’re protecting public trust,” Woods said. “And we understood that the longer this kept going on, we were going to see an erosion in public trust from the people who live, work and play in the city of Tempe.”

Federal lawmakers have also raised alarm over the reported abuse of Flock data.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), the chair of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, launched an investigation into the company’s operations this week, alleging a “woeful lack of safeguards in these systems.”

Earlier this month, Flock added new privacy guidelines to its camera systems, including reducing the default video retention period, adding more methods to detect suspicious searches and providing greater product transparency.

articles.title: Byron Donalds shuts down Bill Maher’s claim on GOP primary racism, says 'Florida is a meritocracy'
articles.summary: Byron Donalds pushed back on Bill Maher's claims that racism cost him key Florida Panhandle counties, calling the state a meritocracy on "Real Time."
articles.body: Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds rejected comedian Bill Maher’s claims that he lost key counties in the recent primary in part due to the racism within the state. Appearing on HBO's "Real Time with Bill Maher" Friday night, Donalds, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, pushed back on host Bill Maher's assertion that he lost parts of Florida's Panhandle because of the area's predominantly White electorate. "You did lose the ‘Redneck Riviera’ badly," Maher said, referring to Donalds’ losses in Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hardee, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Levy, Liberty, Madison, Suwannee, Taylor, Union, and Washington counties — rural counties where roughly 94% of Republican voters are White. STEPHEN A SMITH ADMITS BYRON DONALDS COULD MAKE HIM A REPUBLICAN, CALLS HIM ‘THE REAL DEAL’ "I can’t get with you on a lot of this policy stuff," Maher continued. "But I think it would be great if the country did have [its] first Black, Republican governor." Maher went on to praise Donalds for his willingness to run in "this post-racial world" where constituents don’t care about the "color of their skin," but he added that "we’re not quite there yet though." BILL MAHER BLASTS CALIFORNIA'S EDUCATION RESULTS, CITES TWO SURGING RED STATES "The Redneck Riviera, which is the Panhandle," Maher began. "I think there are people there who still would not — you’re a Republican, you’re a Trumper — they should love you and they don’t. I think there is still racism." "Let’s talk a little bit about the Panhandle," Donalds replied, beginning his rebuttal. "There are counties we did incredibly well in that we won. There were some counties that we fell a little short in, that’s okay." WATCH: BYRON DONALDS BRUSHES OFF GOP DEBATE DEMANDS AS RIVALS LAG FAR BEHIND IN POLLS Donalds then pointed out the crowded Florida primary field which had 11 Republicans on the ballot, with candidates "who had various lines of support." "The number one thing overall, we closed out 48% of the vote in Florida," Donalds said. "800,000 votes [is] a long way to becoming the nominee." TRUMP-BACKED NOMINEES DOMINATE PRIMARY CONTESTS AS PRESIDENT TIGHTENS PARTY VICE GRIP Donalds went on to push back against Maher's argument that racial bias influenced the primary results, insisting that Florida is a place where people can pursue opportunities in elected office. "Florida really has become the microcosm of what we all want," Donalds said. "It's a meritocracy. And it's about the best person with the best views, the best skills, the best talent moving forward to represent your state or to represent a district in your state, and Florida exemplifies that." GIANNO CALDWELL: FLORIDA NEEDS BYRON DONALDS TO PROTECT THE DESANTIS LEGACY However, former Florida state Sen. Dave Aronberg was not as quick to attribute Donalds' showing to the crowded primary field. "When you look at the primary numbers, Byron Donalds falling short of 50% does raise some legitimate questions," Aronberg told Fox News Digital. "Yes, there were 11 names on the ballot, but few of his opponents were viable contenders, and Donalds had a massive fundraising and name recognition advantage compared to the rest of the field. It wasn't exactly a neck-and-neck dogfight." FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME Aronberg added, "When you see him underperforming in certain rural pockets, it's hard to completely dismiss race having played at least some quiet role." "Going into November, Republicans have a massive advantage in party registration and financial resources. But this will be no cakewalk based on what we saw in the primary, along with President Trump’s lagging poll numbers and the quality of his Democratic opponent." ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES Maher later challenged Donalds on his campaign platform by pointing to President Donald Trump’s tariffs impacting affordability across the country — especially in Florida. "I don't feel like the president's policies are making that affordable part easy for you," Maher said. A POPULAR COCKTAIL HAS A TRUMP TRADE PROBLEM YOU PROBABLY DIDN’T KNOW ABOUT "Even the Wall Street Journal, which is usually pretty far right, calls this trade war with Canada the ‘dumbest trade war,’ that's the title," Maher continued. "It says Republicans are already getting pounded on the campaign trail over his tariffs and inflation, mostly because of the war. Byron, are you getting pounded on the campaign trail?" "I think that people in Florida are thinking about their pocketbooks. Well, that's like anywhere else," Donalds said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE He went on to defend Trump’s tariffs on Canada, adding that the president is reevaluating trade policies that are not working for the American people. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But I would rather have a chief executive that looks at these deals and engages these other countries and fights for Americans, [rather] than just lets them roll knowing that they're not gonna be in the interest of small businesses," Donalds said.

articles.title: Electric vehicles are flaming out —let’s ‘Make Internal Combustion Engines Great Again’
articles.summary: If you are a builder, promoter or buyer of electric vehicles, good for you. Science and technology do march on. But occasionally, at what cost? While it’s quite easy to understand the rationale for building EVs — perceived innovation, business plans, and profit — it’s still natural to question the promotion and purchasing of said vehicles. At least for some. Much of the EV market is still wrapped…
articles.body:
If you are a builder, promoter or buyer of electric vehicles, good for you. Science and technology do march on. But occasionally, at what cost?

While it’s quite easy to understand the rationale for building EVs — perceived innovation, business plans, and profit — it’s still natural to question the promotion and purchasing of said vehicles. At least for some.

Much of the EV market is still wrapped around “virtue signaling” as it relates to the ever-moving target of “climate change.” The entitled, lecturing left in Hollywood certainly buys into that narrative, as almost every movie we see these days features an EV or hybrid driven by one of the main characters. “See,” they signal. “We are all about protecting the environment.”

A serious question for Hollywood and the EV huggers is this: what if a percentage of those vehicles are ultimately worse for the environment? Or more costly, more dangerous on the highway, or a fire hazard?

The latter concern was recently the subject in a piece for The Washington Post, titled: “They were told to park outside. Then their cars burst into flames.” But it was the laugh-out-loud sub-headline that betrayed the lengths some will seemingly go to in order to protect the carefully cultivated myth about electric vehicles. “Modern vehicles don’t need to be moving — or even turned on — to catch fire. That’s fueling lots of safety recalls and tough choices.”

The piece goes on to stress that the danger of these “modern vehicles” —no specific mention of “EVs,” just “electronics” — bursting into flames while not running has grown so high that “park outside” warnings have increased into the millions. That’s right, millions.

Leaving aside the “burst into flames” issue associated are a number of other negatives that many on the left prefer we not address. Let’s start with the battery that powers these “modern vehicles.” When being disposed of, these batteries are considered “toxic” and a “hazardous waste.”

The weight of one of these flammable batteries starts at 600 pounds, with the high end topping out around 3,000 pounds. Just the battery. Just like the tens of thousands of “green” wind turbines desecrating the American landscape while killing thousands of birds , the deeper you dive into the details, the more alarming the reality becomes.

Of course, the greatest irony of the “green” energy revolution, be it windmills, solar panels or electric vehicles, is that much of it has to vampire off fossil fuels to be created and, ultimately, to survive. Another fact some on the left would prefer remains unsaid.

But going back to the “modern vehicle” issue, we should never forget that it sure seemed that the “environmentalists” in the Biden administration were seeking to sabotage — or outright destroy — the gasoline-powered car market by forcing a 56 percent reduction in new vehicle emissions by 2032, with the goal of having 60 percent of all new vehicles to electric by 2030 . What could possibly go wrong by taking all internal combustion-powered vehicles offline?

It turns out that upwards of 75 percent of EV battery components are made in — you guessed it — China. Pardon the pun, but forcing the U.S. population into EVs will only put the leadership of China more firmly in the driver’s seat of world domination.

Moving beyond the fire hazard of these EV batteries, their toxicity, the damage their tremendous weight does to tires and roads, and their unreliability in very cold and very hot weather, we come to a serious issue of national and personal security issue: the Biden administration’s attempt to install “kill switches” into all “modern vehicles” as a way to prevent drunk driving.

In January, Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky posted on X : “Federal law says new cars after 2026 must monitor drivers and shut down if the car disapproves. Your dashboard should not be judge, jury, and executioner.”

Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis then amplified this position with his own post on X : “The idea that the federal government would require auto manufacturers to equip cars with a ‘kill switch’ that can be controlled by the government is something you’d expect in Orwell’s 1984, and yet…”

The obvious question in the minds of DeSantis, Massie and millions of other Americans: Who is in charge of this “kill switch?” What if the “nanny state” targets certain individuals, groups or political parties? If you don’t believe this possible, simply cast your mind back to the draconian dictates that came out of the COVID-19 panic.

All of which begs the most important question of all: What was wrong with our “old fashioned” vehicles? Our gasoline-powered cars and the internal combustion engine? Absolutely nothing.

Is there a place for electric vehicles? Of course. They are a wave of the future, but they should not come to represent the whole ocean. We need to hedge our “modern vehicle” bets.

With each passing day, internal combustion powered vehicles continue to prove themselves attractive, valuable and needed. They are generally less expensive than EVs, less likely to spontaneously burst into flames, more reliable in blackouts and weather extremes, and more protective of civil liberties. Not to mention the basic need to transport oneself from Point A to Point B.

While some loudly sing the praises of the “modern vehicle.” I say, “Make Internal Combustion Engines Great Again.” Old may not only be new again — it might literally help to preserve our liberties while protecting our lives.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: The Memo: GOP sees risks in Trump’s midterm strategy of focusing on himself
articles.summary: President Trump is likely to make the GOP’s midterm campaign partly about himself — and that’s a risky strategy, as even some in his party acknowledge. Trump’s efforts go beyond the standard, campaign-trail appearances he is making on behalf of Republican candidates. According to a Tuesday report from The Atlantic, the president has proposed to…
articles.body:
President Trump is likely to make the GOP’s midterm campaign partly about himself — and that’s a risky strategy, as even some in his party acknowledge.

Trump’s efforts go beyond the standard, campaign-trail appearances he is making on behalf of Republican candidates.

According to a Tuesday report from The Atlantic , the president has proposed to use at least some of the $400 million that his main super PAC has at its disposal to try to rebut attacks and instead “lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself.”

The magazine further reported: “The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests.”

On one hand, the general approach is not that unusual. Like most modern presidents, Trump is plainly of the belief that he does not get enough credit for his accomplishments. It stands to reason that he would use some money raised by his organization to defend himself on that score.

On the other hand, there are very obvious dangers in tying Republican candidates in competitive states and districts to an unpopular president.

According to The Hill’s data and polling partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump’s job performance elicits disapproval from roughly 58 percent of Americans and approval from just 39 percent.

His approval ratings on some of the key issues facing voters are even worse.

According to the RealClearPolitics (RCP) polling averages, Trump is a startling 41 points underwater on the issue of combatting inflation. A mere 28 percent of Americans approve while 69 percent disapprove. On the war in Iran , 61 percent disapprove and 34 percent approve.

It is debatable at best whether those numbers can be improved upon with adverting focused on the president’s record. But perhaps a more vexing question is whether a Trump-centric midterms campaign will affect turnout to the advantage of Republicans or Democrats — or whether the Trump-love of the former and the Trump-loathing of the latter will in effect cancel each other out.

Trump’s low approval ratings are the byproduct of the detestation of almost all Democrats and heavily negative numbers among independents. In this week’s Economist/YouGov poll, a mere 2 percent of Democrats approved of his performance, while 88 percent “strongly” disapproved. Among independents, just 25 percent approved and 62 percent disapproved.

But, as the primary season this year has shown, Trump’s grip on the GOP remains firm . In the same Economist poll, 80 percent of Republicans approved of how he is doing his job and just 15 percent disapproved.

All of this makes for a complicated calculus for GOP candidates in November.

“There’s not an easy answer,” said Republican strategist Dan Judy, who is sometimes critical of Trump. “If you say, ‘I don’t want him anywhere near here’ you really do risk not getting that turnout boost that you have to have if you want to win. But the flip-side is, if you have an unpopular president tied closely around your neck, that is going to hurt you among swing voters.”

Then there is the broader question of Trump’s record.

On Wednesday, the president somewhat surprisingly amplified a post from Matt Van Swol in which the conservative social media commentator complained that he was “very worried the GOP is sleepwalking toward a midterm reckoning they don’t see coming” and that the party did not appear to “fully grasp how badly they are f‑‑‑ing up right now.”

In apparent riposte to this argument, however, Trump posted a list of purported accomplishments.

The fact that some of those alleged achievements were either contestable (“$5T+ in deregulation savings” — a claim that seems to have its origins in one professor’s essay for a conservative economic group) or highly divisive (“James Comey arrested”) is in a sense beside Trump’s point.

The thesis is simply that an ad campaign focused on Trump’s accomplishments can produce a rising tide that can lift all GOP boats.

Barry Bennett, who served as a senior adviser in Trump’s first presidential run back in 2016, argued that this idea is correct and that it would therefore be “exceedingly helpful” to have such a campaign.

Bennett said, “We literally sealed the border. And if you want to open the border again, just vote the bums back in.” He was referring to Democrats.

Asked whether that argument wasn’t already voiced frequently enough, including by the president himself, Bennett responded: “People don’t read the daily utterances. They watch TV, they watch social media, and we have to tell that story there.”

Democrats, however, are quite happy for Trump to center himself in the forthcoming campaign.

Several Democratic candidates running in competitive Senate races, including Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) and Michigan nominee Abdul El-Sayed, cite Trump frequently, calculating that opposition to him is so entrenched that even the mention of his name is to their advantage.

They won’t have to try too hard, perhaps. On Thursday, amid a tariff fight with Canada, Trump insisted that he was changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“Donald Trump doesn’t understand economics,” El-Sayed had told a crowd at a town hall the previous night. “You get money from daddy, you become a nepo baby and then all of a sudden decide you’re some master businessman.”

The fight for the midterms, like so much else over the past decade, seems sure to become a fight over Trump.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Ex-Hillary Clinton staffer warns Democrats that courting far-left could cost them Jewish voters
articles.summary: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel accused Democratic leadership of pushing Jewish voters out and warned the party risks losing them over antisemitism.
articles.body: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel this week issued a blunt warning to Democratic leadership ahead of the upcoming midterms: Stop minimizing Jewish voters’ concerns, or they’ll walk. Former Hillary Clinton staffer Kaivan Shroff agreed, saying the issue is whether Jewish Democrats will feel like they have to "explain or defend a basic part of their identity to remain in good standing with the party." Appearing on the Atlantic’s "David Frum Show," Nessel accused the Democratic Party of not valuing its Jewish constituents and making them feel less welcome than members of other minority groups. "I think it’s a fundamental mistake for the Democratic Party to think that you can just push Jewish Democrats out and simply replace them with any other population," Nessel told Frum on Wednesday’s podcast episode. DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM Nessel's comments were echoed by Shroff, a media commentator and former digital organizer for Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign. Shroff told Fox News Digital that Democrats risk losing key Jewish voters as the party grapples with internal divisions over its ideological direction. "What Nessel is saying should make Democrats nervous because this isn’t really a debate about Netanyahu or even Israeli policy — it’s about whether Jewish Democrats are starting to feel like they have to explain or defend a basic part of their identity to remain in good standing with the party," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Ironically, Democrats cannot afford to keep shrinking their political tent in the name of expanding it to folks like Hasan Piker — and then act surprised when pieces of the coalition start walking out." Shroff added that Democratic leaders should stop courting socialist-aligned candidates and start shoring up the establishment supporters who have long defended the party — especially ahead of the midterm elections. "Of course, Nessel is a prominent Democrat in Michigan — a state where a lot of this debate has now centered around Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and his affiliation with streamer Hasan Piker, who has made controversial comments that many other Democrats have just condemned as antisemitic," Shroff said. "It’s a critical Senate seat for Democrats to win and they need all their voters and more to show up. So turning off loyal Democrats like Nessel is a huge issue and should be causing major alarm." MICHIGAN'S DEMOCRATIC AG REFUSES TO ATTEND UPCOMING CONVENTION OVER HARASSMENT CONCERNS According to Nessel, Jewish Democrats have felt ostracized by their own party following the attacks in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and accused leadership of cherry-picking issues that are relevant to supporters. "When a Black person says that a phrase that you’re using or the way you’re talking about this issue to me is racist, I’d like you to stop doing it — we respect that," Nessel said on The David Frum podcast. JEWISH HOUSE DEMOCRAT RECALLS COLLEAGUE SAYING THERE IS NO ANTISEMITISM BECAUSE 'ALL THE JEWS ARE RICH' Nessel then pointed to what she said was a discrepancy in how members of her party handle concerns raised by Jewish voters. "This has been an outlier to me," Nessel said. "I have people saying, ‘You are not going to tell us what you deem to be antisemitic. We’ll decide what’s antisemitic. That’s not up for you, the Jewish population, to decide.’" "I find that to be very off-putting and offensive," she continued. "I think that’s totally unacceptable." BATYA UNGAR-SARGON EXPLAINS WHY SO MANY AMERICAN JEWS BECAME DEMS — AND WHY SOME NOW FEEL POLITICALLY HOMELESS Following her condemnation of the Democrats’ treatment of Jewish constituents’ concerns regarding antisemitism, Nessel added that if faced with the choice, she would choose her Jewish heritage over her party affiliation. "If that’s the deal that has to be made, and I’ve been really candid about this, I was Jewish before I was ever Michigan attorney general — I’m going to be Jewish afterwards," Nessel said. MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS "I was Jewish before I was ever a member of the Democratic Party, and if I have to, I’ll be Jewish afterwards too," she continued. Nessel also took aim at Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, for previous comments he made following an attempted terrorist attack on a synagogue in West Bloomfield earlier this year, in which he remarked, "Hurt people do hurt people." MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS "A lot of us perceived that as sort of making excuses for someone that sought to murder over 100 pre-K schoolchildren and that’s the kind of mentality that bothers me a lot," Nessel said. She added that although El-Sayed has met with Jewish leaders in the community, his unwillingness to retract his previous comments is cause for concern and risks amplifying such views. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Nessel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment. Piker previously told his viewers, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews." Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who is Jewish, called out Piker this week in response. In a social media post. She wrote, "This shouldn’t be hard: no community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views. Period," Slotkin continued, "That goes if you’re pro-Israel, pro-Palestine, pro-choice, pro-life or any other cause you care about. And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people."

articles.title: Trump admin unjustly revoked pro-Palestinian foreign students’ visas, judge finds
articles.summary: A federal judge in California ruled Friday the Trump administration unconstitutionally sought to deport international students for pro-Palestinian activism and criticism of Israel. In a 90-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise found the President Trump administration’s use of existing immigration law to cancel foreign students’ visas and deport them violated their constitutional right to…
articles.body:
A federal judge in California ruled Friday the Trump administration unconstitutionally sought to deport international students for pro-Palestinian activism and criticism of Israel.

In a 90-page ruling , U.S. District Judge Noël Wise found the President Trump administration’s use of existing immigration law to cancel foreign students’ visas and deport them violated their constitutional right to free speech.

“In the United States, free speech, including the freedom to criticize the government and its leaders, is not a sign of our democracy’s fragility. It is evidence of its strength,” Wise wrote.

“That strength is diminished when members of our society—citizens and noncitizens alike—must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation,” he continued.

The case stems from a lawsuit filed by Stanford University’s independent student newspaper, The Stanford Daily, last year. The paper claimed some of its writers in the U.S. on student visas had declined to cover pro-Palestinian protests or report on topics related to Israel’s military action in Gaza for fear they would face deportation.

In a legal complaint filed last August, the student paper — along with two anonymous plaintiffs not affiliated with the Daily — accused Secretary of State Marco Rubio and then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem of violating students’ constitutional rights with their immigration enforcement operations.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) , first enacted in 1952, grants the secretary of state the power to authorize a person’s deportation if he determined they jeopardized “a compelling foreign policy interest.”

Wise found that Rubio, along with other White House officials, used this provision to justify retaliation against non-U.S. citizens opposing the government’s stances.

The ruling memo cites several instances in which Trump administration officials labeled pro-Palestinian protesters “sympathizers” of Hamas, the militant group that orchestrated the Oct. 7, 2023, attack in Israel. For the past year and a half, it continues, Trump and his allies repeatedly threatened to deport and revoke visas of college campus demonstration participants.

The document also references a January 2025 White House memo, which read, “To all the resident aliens who joined in the pro-jihadist protests, we put you on notice: come 2025, we will find you, and we will deport you. I will also quickly cancel the student visas of all Hamas sympathizers on college campuses, which have been infested with radicalism like never before.”

Wise, who was appointed by former President Biden to the Northern District of California, sided with the student paper. He found the Trump administration violated students’ First and Fifth Amendments when it relied on two provisions of the INA to use their speech as a basis for deportation.

The Hill has reached out to the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

George Porteous, the student newspaper’s editor-in-chief, celebrated the ruling in a statement shared on social media Friday.

“The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation,” he wrote. “Today’s victory means they won’t have to.”

Attorney Conor Fitzpatrick, whose organization Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression represented the paper in this lawsuit, said in a statement that the ruling “proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

articles.body:
Democrats slammed Friday’s announcement by President Trump on a new deal to acquire majority U.S. control of over 65 million barrels of Venezuelan oil.

“Let’s be clear: this isn’t a win,” Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D) wrote in a social media post .

“This is proof Trump put our service members at risk to get Venezuelan oil for his billionaire buddies,” he continued. “Putting our soldiers’ lives on the line for private profit is a gross dereliction of his constitutional duty.”

Trump announced the deal in a Truth Social post , calling it the “BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY.”

“This Historic Transaction MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves, greatly increases our Oil Supply, and will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity,” the president continued.

This deal applies to around 21 percent of the South American country’s total proven oil reserves, which amount to about 303 billion barrels .

The transaction follows the U.S. military’s capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year and comes amid rising energy costs amid the Iran war. Trump has repeatedly expressed his interest in expanding U.S. investment in Venezuela’s oil industry.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), who serves on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the president of using Maduro’s ouster to “control Venezuelan oil.”

“Will prices come down for Americans? Who knows but likely not as much as Trump has forced them up thru his idiotic Iran War,” Kaine wrote on the social platform X .

“But here’s a guarantee—this will pad the pockets of Trump family and Big Oil companies and delay transition to cleaner energy,” the Virginia Democrat continued. “Bottom line—Using our troops for a private oil grab is corruption at epic scale!”

GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno (Ohio) hit back at Democrats’ criticism of this deal.

“If it were up to DC Democrats, Maduro would still be in power, Venezuelan oil would be going to China at half price, and the people of Venezuela would be getting robbed by a corrupt regime,” the lawmaker wrote on social media . “Instead, this historic deal benefits both countries for generations!”

Venezuela’s acting leader, Delcy Rodriguez, called the deal a “historic milestone in bilateral relations between Venezuela and the U.S.”

“These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere, and greater balance in international markets,” Rodriguez said.

articles.body:
Far-right political figure Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported to the United Kingdom after his detention in Louisiana earlier this week, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody apprehended the British native on Thursday evening at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) in Kenner, La., after DHS officials said he chose to “overstay his welcome” in the United States.

Yiannopoulos — who previously worked on the 2024 presidential campaign for the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West — was in Louisiana for the artist’s scheduled concert.

Federal officials said he “legally entered” the U.S. on May 14 through New York City and was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on July 22 after he failed to show up for an immigration hearing.

DHS deported the British national back to his home country on Friday, a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation.

“DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country,” the spokesperson said. “Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

Yiannopoulos built a reputation as a conservative firebrand in his writing for the far-right Breitbart News, garnering criticism for his incendiary comments about Muslims, women and other groups of people.

In 2017, he stepped down from his role as senior editor at Breitbart after he made comments that appeared to condone pedophilia. Yiannopoulos apologized at the time, but he accused the media of misrepresenting his comments.

During President Trump’s second term, Yiannopoulos has supported the administration’s widespread immigration enforcement operations and called for “total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty.”

“There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering,” he wrote in a social media post last June. “It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

articles.title: Walmart settles DOJ opioid crisis lawsuit for $50 million
articles.summary: Walmart has agreed to pay $50 million to settle a lawsuit claiming that its pharmacies filled hundreds of thousands of illegal prescriptions for controlled substances that fueled the opioid crisis, the Justice Department announced Friday. The settlement resolves a federal lawsuit filed in 2020 that accused the retail giant of failing to report suspicious orders…
articles.body:
Walmart has agreed to pay $50 million to settle a lawsuit claiming that its pharmacies filled hundreds of thousands of illegal prescriptions for controlled substances that fueled the opioid crisis, the Justice Department announced Friday.

The settlement resolves a federal lawsuit filed in 2020 that accused the retail giant of failing to report suspicious orders at its pharmacies to the Drug Enforcement Agency.

The government alleged that Walmart’s compliance team knowingly filled invalid prescriptions written by prescribers operating as “pill mills” even after pharmacists raised concerns about them.

“Over an approximately four-year period, a time during which Walmart shipped an estimated 37.5 million controlled-substance orders to its pharmacies, it reported only 204 suspicious orders to D.E.A. — in other words, almost none,” according to court documents.

As part of the settlement, Walmart will create a hotline for workers and patients to report suspected illegal dispensing of controlled substances. The company will also monitor dispensing activity at its pharmacies and establish a system to review doctors that are suspected of improper prescribing.

“This $50 million settlement makes clear that pharmacies have a responsibility to identify and prevent the unlawful dispensing of controlled substances,” DEA assistant administrator Cheri Oz said in a statement. “Filling illegitimate opioid prescriptions puts patients and communities at risk and undermines the safeguards designed to prevent the diversion and misuse of potentially addictive medications.”

Oz added, “This settlement addresses past conduct while establishing clear compliance obligations designed to strengthen safeguards and help prevent these failures from happening again.”

This is the latest opioid-related settlement involving Walmart, the world’s largest retail chain.

In 2022, the company agreed to pay $1.3 billion to settle thousands of lawsuits brought by states that accused its pharmacies of contributing to the opioid crisis.

Other major pharmacy operators have reached similar settlements, including Kroger, which agreed in 2023 to pay $1.2 billion to states and local governments over its handling of prescriptions.

About 806,000 people have died from overdoses involving prescription drugs between 1999 and 2023, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
